newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU leaning towards plan to limit risk ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU leaning towards plan to limit risk ahead of EMU.

text.p: Recognising the power that speculators have to create currency turmoil, European Union authorities are looking at how to minimise the risks in the run-up to the launch of a common currency.

Past currency upheavals, such as in September 1992 when Britain and Italy were forced out of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism, have focused attention on how to smooth the transition towards economic and monetary union (EMU).

At issue is the critical period between early 1998, when the EU will decide which countries qualify for EMU, and January 1, 1999 when the common euro currency is launched. Then the currencies of EMU members will become "irrevocably" fixed.

Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of Europe's future central bank -- the European Monetary Institute -- has tried to defuse market speculation about conversion rates by arguing they should fixed by averaging past rates between EMU currencies. The length of the averaging process -- six months, a year, or two years -- would still have to be decided.
It is an idea which is gaining ground among EU officials.
As one EU monetary official put it: "If they know in advance what the calculation will be, it's more likely that speculation would be constructive...converging rather than diverging."
The averaging technique could be announced to financial markets when EMU members are chosen.
While the Maastricht Treaty that governs the single currency process allows rates to be fixed only on January 1, 1999 -- announcing the method would dispel market uncertainty.
The issue was informally discussed by some of those attending a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin last weekend.
Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told reporters that Lamfalussy had proposed announcing an averaging approach at the same time as a decision is taken on EMU participants.
While the matter is not currently under discussion by either the European Commission or the EU's Monetary Committee, some officials predict it will win support.

"Our own thinking is that there is not substantial opposition," said one official, adding that the only ones who might object are countries which might want to engage in a "last-minute devaluation" ahead of the start of EMU.

While the plan could go a long way towards reducing speculative activity on the foreign exchange markets, some say an announcement could signal that central banks of EMU nations were less than prepared to defend a given set of parity rates.

Christopher Taylor, an economist at the National Institute of Economic Research in London, said there were basically two options for dealing with the key period before the single currency is launched.
"The issue is between a pre-announcement of the fixed set of rates and some sort of formula," Taylor said.
A third option, the one laid out in the treaty, would be to accept market rates on January 1, 1999. Few, however, seem prepared to go that route.
Under the first approach, EMU members would announce the central parity rates between currencies they were ready to defend, creating a sort of de facto monetary union.
Assuming a close degree of convergence, the parity rates might be very near to those which currently exist.
This would be a bold step, and some say it would put the German Bundesbank in a very uncomfortable spot. Essentially, the central bank would have to be prepared to engage in unlimited intervention.
An alternative would be Lamfalussy's plan, which Taylor says lets governments off the hook a bit but might also signal to markets that something could go wrong.
"The question is still what if there is some unforeseen event," he added. "I think it boils down to whether there would be some exogenous occurence."

A sharp rise in U.S. interest rates, a war, or some other form of external shock would put EU monetary authorities on the defensive. An averaging technique could make management of a crisis a bit easier, say analysts.
